native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 respondents, family net wealth of the non-black non-Hispanic cohort - used here as a PROXY for 'white', because this dataset encodes race/ethnicity only as the 1979 racial/ethnic cohort (1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC, 3=NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC) and contains no strict non-Hispanic white identifier - exceeded that of black and Hispanic respondents at the median in every wave in which wealth is observed, and the gap widened between 1985 and 1996. The white-proxy/black median wealth ratio rose from about 2.2x in 1985 (USD 3,500 vs 1,600) to 2.7x in 1990 (12,972 vs 4,800) and 4.3x in 1996 (42,600 vs 9,800), a 1996/1985 ratio-of-ratios of 2.0 (95% CI 1.7-2.5); the white-proxy/Hispanic ratio rose from 7.0x (3,500 vs 500) to 8.1x (12,972 vs 1,600) and 16.6x (42,600 vs 2,562), a ratio-of-ratios of 2.4 (95% CI 1.9-3.1). Because median wealth grew for all three groups, both the relative and the absolute gaps widened: the median difference over the white-proxy group grew from about USD 1,900 (black) and 3,000 (Hispanic) in 1985 to about 32,800 and 40,000 (1996 dollars) in 1996. The rank ordering white-proxy > black > Hispanic was stable in all three waves, and the widening is reproduced in a balanced panel of the 5,739 respondents observed in all waves and when parental-household residents are excluded, so it is not driven by composition or by the 1996 non-response (52.6% missing in the reference cohort vs 31.7%/33.4%). Means and p99-Winsorised means show smaller ratios (roughly 1.9-2.9x vs black, 3.1-6.4x vs Hispanic) than the medians, indicating the median gap is not an artefact of top-coded wealthy tails. This conclusion rests on three unweighted observational waves of family-level (not individual) net wealth with a coarse racial/ethnic proxy and 15-53% item missingness per cell, so it describes an association and its trajectory over 1985-1996, not a causal mechanism, and should not be read as U.S.-population estimates.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Derived race/ethnicity groups from `Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979` (3=non-black non-Hispanic, proxy for white; 1=black; 2=Hispanic) - no explicit white/black/Hispanic variables exist in the file. 2) Reshaped the three available wealth waves (1985, 1990, 1996; no wealth variables exist for any other year) to long format; complete cases per cell, no imputation of wealth. 3) Primary estimator = median family net wealth per group x year with percentile bootstrap CIs (2,000 replicates, seed 20261025), reporting N and missing rate next to every median. 4) Primary contrasts = within-year ratios (inflation-invariant) plus absolute differences in levels, with cell-wise bootstrap CIs. 5) Respondent-level (cluster) bootstrap resampling each respondent's whole panel (seed 7) to obtain CIs for the cross-year change (ratio-of-ratios 1996/1985) while respecting within-person correlation. 6) Sensitivity analyses (not primary): excluding respondents living in parental households (residence codes 17/18/19), a balanced panel of the 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves, arithmetic means and p99-Winsorised means (tails are top-coded at 1,054,132 / 1,321,099 / 1,232,183). 7) Secondary deflated column converts mediles/differences to 1996 dollars with HARDCODED CPI-U annual-average deflators (1985=107.6, 1990=130.7, 1996=156.9, BLS); the CPI does NOT come from the dataset, which is why within-year ratios are the headline metric. 8) The file contains no survey weights, strata or PSUs, so all estimates are sample-based, not U.S.-population estimates.
